flowers.taxonomicNote: Kew's Plants of the World Online currently accepts Nymphaea nouchali var. caerulea (Savigny) Verdc. and treats Nymphaea caerulea Savigny as a synonym. The common name 'Blue Lotus' refers to this water-lily taxon; it is not a true lotus in the genus Nelumbo.
flowers.growthForm: Rhizomatous hydrogeophyte — an aquatic plant that persists through an underground rhizome.

morphology.leaves: Leaves are generally round to elliptic, borne on long petioles, with a basal notch and prominent veins on the underside.
morphology.flowers: Flowers are blue or pinkish and about 8–12 cm across in the Flora Zambesiaca treatment cited by Kew; a 2023 review describes flowers around 15–20 cm in some cultivated/observed material, illustrating geographic or source-dependent variation.
morphology.petals: Typically 14–20 petals are described for the taxon in Flora Zambesiaca.
morphology.stamens: The flowers have very numerous stamens, around 100–200 or more in the cited Flora Zambesiaca description.
morphology.fruit: The fruit is depressed-globose; cited specimens are around 2.2 × 3.2 cm.
morphology.seeds: Seeds are small and ellipsoid, about 1.2 mm long in the cited description.

interestingFacts.title: It is not a true lotus
interestingFacts.text: Despite the common name, Blue Lotus belongs to Nymphaea, the water-lily genus. True lotuses belong to the separate genus Nelumbo.

interestingFacts.title: Its scientific name has a taxonomic history
interestingFacts.text: Nymphaea caerulea was published by Savigny in 1798. Kew currently treats that name as a synonym of Nymphaea nouchali var. caerulea.

interestingFacts.title: A flower packed with stamens
interestingFacts.text: The Flora Zambesiaca description cited by Kew records approximately 100–200 or more stamens in a flower.

interestingFacts.title: The visible flower is only part of the plant
interestingFacts.text: The plant is rhizomatous: much of its structure remains beneath the water, while long petioles connect the submerged base to leaves and flowers at the surface.

interestingFacts.title: A flower with an ancient visual history
interestingFacts.text: Blue lotus imagery appears repeatedly in ancient Egyptian art, including objects and funerary contexts from the New Kingdom and earlier periods.

culturalNotes.title: Ancient Egyptian imagery
culturalNotes.text: Blue water-lily imagery is extensively documented in ancient Egyptian art and objects. The Walters Art Museum identifies Nymphaea caerulea in New Kingdom aquatic imagery and notes associations with rebirth and regeneration.

culturalNotes.title: Funerary and ceremonial contexts
culturalNotes.text: Museum records document blue-lotus forms and imagery in Egyptian objects, including lotus-shaped chalices and funerary material. The Metropolitan Museum records Nymphaea caerulea as blue water lily material associated with a Third Intermediate Period burial context.

culturalNotes.title: A historical meaning, not a universal definition
culturalNotes.text: Historical associations such as renewal and rebirth belong to particular Egyptian cultural contexts. Sunday Garden presents them as documented cultural history rather than a universal meaning that every Gardener must share.

symbolism: renewal and rebirth in documented ancient Egyptian contexts
flowers.sundayGardenInterpretation: A flower can carry its roots beneath the surface without being defined by the water around them. The Blue Lotus becomes a Sunday Garden metaphor for moving through what shaped you, finding the surface, and choosing to bloom without pretending the water was always clear.

distribution.nativeRange: Egypt to southern Africa, the southern Arabian Peninsula, and the Comoros.
distribution.introducedElsewhere: Kew records introductions in parts of South America, South Asia, the Pacific, and Australasia.
distribution.distributionNote: The native range is distinct from places where the taxon has been introduced.

habitatProfile.habitat: Wet tropical environments and freshwater habitats.
habitatProfile.growthEnvironment: Primarily associated with wet tropical biomes and freshwater aquatic environments.
habitatProfile.growthForm: Rhizomatous hydrogeophyte — an aquatic plant that persists through an underground rhizome.

flowering.flowerPosition: Flowers are held at or above the water surface.
flowering.flowerSize: About 8–12 cm across in the Flora Zambesiaca description cited by Kew.
flowering.colour: Blue or pinkish in the cited Flora Zambesiaca treatment.

reproduction.flowers: Flowers contain numerous stamens and multiple carpels; the cited Flora Zambesiaca description records about 100–200 or more stamens and 14–24 carpels.
reproduction.fruit: The fruit is depressed-globose in the cited description.
reproduction.seeds: Seeds are small and ellipsoid, about 1.2 mm long in the cited description.
reproduction.note: These reproductive details describe the documented morphology; the page does not infer a specific pollinator or pollination mechanism without a source.

lifeCycle.persistence: It is a rhizomatous hydrogeophyte, meaning the plant persists through a rhizome while its leaves and flowers occupy the aquatic surface zone.
lifeCycle.seasonalityNote: Exact flowering season can vary with geography and growing conditions, so Sunday Garden does not assign a single universal flowering season.

ecology.role: A freshwater aquatic flowering plant rooted in submerged substrate, with leaves and flowers extending toward the water surface.
ecology.caution: The audit does not assign a single specialised pollinator or ecological role without direct source support.

conservation.note: This record does not assign a global conservation status without a directly applicable assessment for the accepted infraspecific taxon. Native and introduced distributions are kept separate.

phases.name: Phase 01
phases.description: A rhizome anchors the plant in the substrate beneath the water.

phases.name: Phase 02
phases.description: Long petioles carry leaves upward until their blades reach the water surface.

phases.name: Phase 03
phases.description: Flowers are held at or above the water surface.

phases.name: Phase 04
phases.description: The plant persists as a rhizomatous hydrogeophyte; exact seasonal timing varies with geography and growing conditions.

flowers.taxonomicNote: Red Rose is a common colour-based description rather than a single botanical species. Roses sold or described as red may belong to many species, hybrids, and cultivated groups within Rosa, so this profile uses genus-level botanical information and does not assign one species to the Gardener's flower.
flowers.growthForm: Woody shrubs or climbing plants; stems may be upright, arching, scrambling, trailing, or climbing, and are commonly armed with prickles.

morphology.roots: Roses are woody perennial plants with root systems that anchor the plant and support long-lived stems; exact root architecture varies among species and cultivated roses.
morphology.stem: Stems and branches are commonly armed with prickles and may be upright, arching, scrambling, trailing, or climbing.
morphology.leaves: Leaves are typically compound and imparipinnate, with serrated leaflets and stipules associated with the leaf bases.
morphology.flowers: Rose flowers are bisexual and may occur singly or in clusters such as corymbs. In the genus Rosa, flowers typically have five sepals and five petals in wild species, while cultivated roses may have many additional petals through selection and breeding.
morphology.fruit: After pollination and maturation, the floral receptacle develops into the familiar rose hip, a fleshy structure enclosing numerous achenes.
morphology.prickles: Rosa stems are commonly described as bearing prickles; these are often casually called thorns in everyday language, but botanical descriptions distinguish them from true thorns.

interestingFacts.title: Red Rose is not one species
interestingFacts.text: The phrase Red Rose describes flower colour, not a single species. The genus Rosa contains many species and a very large diversity of cultivated hybrids and selections.

interestingFacts.title: Roses are prickly, not technically thorny
interestingFacts.text: Kew describes Rosa stems and branches as usually having prickles and/or thorns in its genus treatment, while horticultural sources commonly use 'thorns' in everyday language. The distinction can depend on the botanical context.

interestingFacts.title: Rose hips are fruits
interestingFacts.text: Many roses form hips after flowering. The hip develops from the flower's receptacle and contains numerous achenes; hips can persist into autumn and provide food for birds in some landscapes.

interestingFacts.title: Wild roses and cultivated roses are very different in form
interestingFacts.text: Roses range from simple five-petalled wild flowers to highly selected modern cultivars with complex flower forms, including rosettes and many-petalled blooms.

interestingFacts.title: Colour does not define the taxonomy
interestingFacts.text: A red-flowered rose can belong to different species or cultivated lineages. Colour alone is therefore not enough to identify a rose botanically.

culturalNotes.title: Love and romantic imagery
culturalNotes.text: Roses have long been associated with love and beauty in European and Mediterranean cultural traditions. Museum and historical sources document the rose as a recurring emblem of romantic love, while the exact meaning depends on period and context.

culturalNotes.title: Medieval heraldry
culturalNotes.text: The rose became a prominent heraldic emblem in medieval Europe. The Metropolitan Museum of Art notes associations ranging from the Virgin Mary and the Five Wounds of Christ to romantic love, showing that the flower carried multiple meanings rather than one universal definition.

culturalNotes.title: The red and white roses of English history
culturalNotes.text: The red rose became associated with the House of Lancaster while the white rose was associated with the House of York in the fifteenth-century conflict later called the Wars of the Roses. The Tudor rose subsequently combined red and white imagery.

culturalNotes.title: Victorian language of flowers
culturalNotes.text: Victorian floriography assigned messages to flowers and flower colours. Smithsonian material records the red rose as a sign of passionate love within that particular nineteenth-century symbolic system.

culturalNotes.title: A symbol shaped by context
culturalNotes.text: Historical sources show the rose appearing in religious art, heraldry, romantic imagery, literature, and political or national symbolism. Sunday Garden therefore treats symbolism as culturally situated rather than as a fixed botanical meaning.

symbolism: romantic love — documented especially in European and Victorian traditions
passionate love — documented in Victorian floriography
beauty and desire — recurring cultural associations
strength and vulnerability — an interpretive pairing often drawn from the contrast between the flower and prickly stems
heritage and allegiance — documented in medieval and English heraldic history
flowers.sundayGardenInterpretation: The Red Rose can be read as a meeting point between openness and boundaries. Its flower invites attention through colour, form, and fragrance, while its prickly stems remind us that beauty does not require unlimited access. In Sunday Garden, that contrast can become a metaphor for someone who is willing to be seen, to feel deeply, and still to know where their boundaries are.

distribution.nativeRange: The genus Rosa is native across temperate and subtropical parts of the Northern Hemisphere.
distribution.introducedElsewhere: Individual cultivated roses have been introduced and grown far beyond the native ranges of their source species; distribution therefore varies by species and cultivar.
distribution.distributionNote: Because Red Rose is a colour category rather than one species, no single native range can be assigned to it. Kew's genus-level treatment gives a Northern Hemisphere native range for Rosa.

habitatProfile.habitat: Rosa species occupy a wide range of habitats, including woodland edges, scrub, grassland, hedgerows, and other temperate or subtropical environments, depending on species.
habitatProfile.growthEnvironment: Cultivated roses generally perform best in fertile, moisture-retentive but well-drained soil and sunny positions, while wild species have species-specific ecological requirements.
habitatProfile.growthForm: Woody perennial shrubs, climbers, ramblers, trailers, and related forms within Rosa.

flowering.flowerPosition: Flowers may be solitary or borne in clusters such as corymbs, depending on species and cultivar.
flowering.flowerSize: Size varies considerably among species and cultivars, so no single size is assigned to Red Rose as a colour category.
flowering.colour: Red is one of the many flower colours found across cultivated roses; the precise shade ranges from crimson and scarlet to darker red tones depending on cultivar.

reproduction.flowers: Flowers are bisexual in the general Rosa genus description, with numerous stamens and multiple carpels.
reproduction.fruit: After flowering, the receptacle can enlarge into a rose hip containing numerous achenes.
reproduction.seeds: Seeds are contained within the hip as achenes; seed production and fruiting vary with species, cultivar, pollination, and whether spent flowers are removed.
reproduction.note: The genus contains both wild species and extensively bred cultivars, so reproductive biology can differ among roses. This profile avoids assigning a single pollination mechanism to every Red Rose.

lifeCycle.persistence: Roses are woody perennial plants. Individual plants can persist for years while producing seasonal shoots, leaves, flowers, and, when allowed, hips.
lifeCycle.seasonalityNote: Flowering season varies by species, climate, and cultivar. Some roses flower in one main flush, while others can flower repeatedly through the growing season.

ecology.role: Wild and cultivated roses can contribute flowers and fruits to garden and wider plant communities. Rose hips are eaten by birds and can help distribute seeds in some species.
ecology.caution: Ecological relationships vary among Rosa species and cultivars, so this entry does not assign one universal pollinator or ecological role to every Red Rose.

conservation.note: A conservation status cannot be assigned to 'Red Rose' as a colour category. Individual wild Rosa species have their own distributions and conservation assessments, while cultivated roses are managed horticultural plants.

phases.name: Phase 01
phases.description: A rose establishes a perennial woody framework from which new shoots arise.

phases.name: Phase 02
phases.description: Depending on the species or cultivar, growth may form a shrub, climber, rambler, groundcover, or compact container plant.

phases.name: Phase 03
phases.description: Leaves develop along the shoots and flowers are produced on new or established flowering growth, with flowering behaviour varying substantially among rose groups.

phases.name: Phase 04
phases.description: If flowers are allowed to mature rather than being removed, many roses develop hips containing seeds.

flowers.taxonomicNote: Pink Tulip is a descriptive colour category, not a single botanical species. Pink flowers occur across cultivated tulips and can also occur in different species and hybrids. This record therefore uses the accepted genus Tulipa rather than assigning one species without evidence.
flowers.growthForm: Bulbous geophyte — tulips persist through an underground bulb and produce seasonal above-ground leaves, stems and flowers.

morphology.bulb: Tulips grow from fleshy underground bulbs covered by a papery outer skin. The bulb stores resources for the next season.
morphology.roots: Roots arise from the basal region of the bulb and support water and nutrient uptake after growth begins.
morphology.leaves: Leaves are generally broad to narrow and strap-like, usually green to grey-green, and arise from the base of the plant.
morphology.stem: Flowering stems rise above the foliage and commonly carry a single terminal flower in cultivated tulips, although form varies across the genus.
morphology.flower: Tulip flowers vary greatly in size, shape and colour. Cup-shaped flowers are common, while cultivated forms include lily-flowered, fringed, parrot and peony-flowered types.
morphology.fruit: After successful reproduction, a capsule can develop and contain seeds; many cultivated tulips are instead propagated vegetatively for reliable cultivar characteristics.

interestingFacts.title: Pink is not a species name
interestingFacts.text: A pink tulip can belong to many cultivated tulip groups or species. Colour alone does not identify one species, which is why Sunday Garden keeps the record at Tulipa spp.

interestingFacts.title: Tulipa is a large genus
interestingFacts.text: Kew currently lists Tulipa as an accepted genus and its Plants of the World Online treatment includes 95 accepted species.

interestingFacts.title: Tulips have underground storage
interestingFacts.text: The visible flower is seasonal; the plant persists through a bulb that stores resources between periods of above-ground growth.

interestingFacts.title: Cultivated forms are remarkably diverse
interestingFacts.text: RHS groups cultivated tulips into forms including lily-flowered, fringed, parrot and peony-flowered types, showing how much variation exists within the genus.

interestingFacts.title: Some tulips multiply naturally
interestingFacts.text: RHS notes that specialist tulips closely related to wild species often multiply in gardens, while many border tulips are less reliable at reflowering in their second year.

interestingFacts.title: A pink form has been recorded within T. gesneriana
interestingFacts.text: Kew records Tulipa gesneriana var. rosea as a synonym of Tulipa gesneriana. This is one documented example of why a pink tulip should not automatically be treated as its own species.

culturalNotes.title: Ottoman floral culture
culturalNotes.text: Tulips became important motifs in Ottoman visual culture. The Metropolitan Museum documents tulips among the stylized floral motifs used on Iznik ceramics and Ottoman textiles.

culturalNotes.title: The Tulip Period
culturalNotes.text: The reign of Ahmed III (1703–1730) is commonly called the Tulip Period; the Metropolitan Museum notes that the flower’s popularity was reflected in floral decoration across textiles, illumination and architecture.

culturalNotes.title: Arrival in western Europe
culturalNotes.text: The Metropolitan Museum records that tulips were imported into the Netherlands from Turkey in the 1580s and that Carolus Clusius helped establish their cultivation at Leiden.

culturalNotes.title: Tulipomania and historical nuance
culturalNotes.text: Seventeenth-century Dutch fascination with rare tulips included intense speculation around particular bulbs. Museum and historical accounts often call this episode Tulipomania; later scholarship has challenged simplified stories that portray it as a straightforward economy-wide mania.

culturalNotes.title: A decorative language across cultures
culturalNotes.text: Museum collections show tulip motifs appearing in Ottoman ceramics, textiles and other decorative arts, while European botanical art later documented and celebrated cultivated tulip varieties.

symbolism: passion — documented in a Smithsonian Gardens language-of-flowers resource
beauty and cultivated variety — interpretive rather than a universal botanical meaning
renewal and seasonal return — Sunday Garden interpretation based on the plant’s seasonal growth cycle
flowers.sundayGardenInterpretation: A tulip reminds us that a visible bloom can come from something that spends much of its life beneath the surface. Its colour may be soft, vivid, unusual or ordinary, but the flower does not need to explain its shade before it is allowed to bloom. Pink Tulip, in particular, is not one fixed botanical identity; it is a colour shared across many cultivated forms. That makes it a fitting Sunday Garden metaphor for people who may share a feeling while carrying completely different stories. The flower is recognizable from a distance, but the life behind the bloom is always more specific.

distribution.nativeRange: The genus Tulipa is native across a broad region from south-central and eastern Europe through the Mediterranean region to Mongolia, according to Kew.
distribution.introducedElsewhere: Kew records Tulipa as introduced in several regions outside its native range, including parts of western and northern Europe, North America and Korea.
distribution.distributionNote: These ranges apply to the genus Tulipa, not specifically to every pink-flowered cultivated tulip. Cultivars may have complex horticultural histories and are widely grown outside the genus’s native range.

habitatProfile.habitat: Tulipa species occupy a variety of terrestrial habitats across their native range, while cultivated tulips are commonly grown in gardens, borders, rock gardens and containers.
habitatProfile.growthEnvironment: Many cultivated tulips perform best with good drainage, full sun and a seasonal pattern that provides cool, moist growth conditions followed by a relatively dry summer rest.

flowering.flowerPosition: Flowers are borne on upright stems, commonly singly at the top of the stem in cultivated tulips.
flowering.flowerSize: Size varies substantially among species and cultivars; no single universal size is assigned to the Pink Tulip category.
flowering.colour: Pink is one of many flower colours found in cultivated tulips; colour intensity and pattern vary among cultivars.
flowering.season: Most garden tulips flower in mid to late spring, although timing varies with cultivar, species and climate.

reproduction.sexual: Tulips can reproduce sexually by seed. Specialist tulips are more commonly propagated this way than many border cultivars.
reproduction.vegetative: Tulips can also multiply through offsets — young bulbs that form around the parent bulb. This is especially useful for maintaining cultivated forms.
reproduction.note: Seed-grown tulips can take several years to reach flowering size, while offsets provide a way to clone or increase established bulbs more predictably.

lifeCycle.persistence: The bulb allows the plant to survive periods when leaves and flowers are absent. Above-ground growth emerges seasonally, flowers, then the foliage dies back after replenishing the bulb.
lifeCycle.seasonalityNote: Exact timing depends on species, cultivar and climate. RHS describes most garden tulips as flowering in mid to late spring and notes a summer dormant period for many tulips.

ecology.role: Tulips are terrestrial flowering plants that contribute seasonal flowers and reproductive resources to their local environments. Exact ecological interactions vary among species and regions.
ecology.caution: Because Pink Tulip is a broad horticultural category, this record does not assign one universal pollinator, habitat community or ecological role to every pink-flowered tulip.

conservation.note: No single conservation status is assigned here because Pink Tulip is a horticultural colour category rather than one species. Conservation needs differ among wild Tulipa species; cultivated tulips should not be treated as a proxy for the status of their wild relatives.
conservation.wildSpeciesNote: Kew’s genus-level treatment contains many accepted species, including species with restricted native ranges. Conservation assessment should therefore be performed at species level when discussing a particular wild tulip.

phases.name: Phase 01
phases.description: The bulb remains dormant through part of the year and stores reserves underground.

phases.name: Phase 02
phases.description: With suitable seasonal conditions, leaves emerge and the plant develops a flowering stem.

phases.name: Phase 03
phases.description: Most cultivated tulips flower in mid to late spring, although flowering time varies by type and climate.

phases.name: Phase 04
phases.description: After flowering, the foliage continues to photosynthesise and replenish the bulb before gradually yellowing and dying back.

phases.name: Phase 05
phases.description: Many specialist tulips can persist and multiply in favourable conditions, while many bedding tulips are treated as seasonal displays because reliable reflowering is not guaranteed.

flowers.taxonomicNote: White Lily is a colour/common-category description rather than a single species. The genus Lilium contains multiple white-flowered species and cultivars. Lilium candidum is one well-documented species whose common names include white lily, but the Gardener entry does not provide enough evidence to identify the flower as that species.
flowers.growthForm: Perennial bulbous geophytes; the genus produces annual leafy shoots from multi-scaled bulbs.

morphology.roots: Perennial roots arise from the bulb; some lilies can also form roots near the stem base.
morphology.bulb: Bulbs are made of overlapping fleshy scales and, unlike tunicate bulbs such as onions, generally lack a complete tunic.
morphology.stem: Stems are generally erect and leafy, usually unbranched.
morphology.leaves: Leaves are simple and parallel-veined, arranged alternately or in whorls depending on species.
morphology.flower: Lilium flowers vary greatly in shape and colour. They may be trumpet-, bowl-, funnel- or Turk’s-cap-shaped; white is one of the colours represented across the genus.
morphology.fruit: The fruit is generally a capsule containing numerous seeds.

interestingFacts.title: White Lily is not one species
interestingFacts.text: The name can describe several white-flowered lilies. The Sunday Garden record therefore stays at the genus level rather than assigning one species without evidence.

interestingFacts.title: Lilium is a true-lily genus
interestingFacts.text: Kew treats Lilium as an accepted genus in Liliaceae. Its native range extends across temperate parts of the Northern Hemisphere to the northern Philippines.

interestingFacts.title: Madonna lily is one specific example
interestingFacts.text: Lilium candidum is an accepted species in Kew and is commonly known as Madonna lily; RHS also lists white lily among its common names.

interestingFacts.title: Lilies have many flower forms
interestingFacts.text: RHS describes trumpet, bowl, funnel-shaped and Turk’s-cap flowers across cultivated lilies, showing why colour alone is not enough to identify a species.

culturalNotes.title: The white lily in European Christian art
culturalNotes.text: White lilies have a long documented association with Christian visual culture, particularly representations of purity and the Virgin Mary. These meanings belong to specific artistic and religious traditions rather than functioning as universal botanical meanings.

culturalNotes.title: Madonna lily as a historical species
culturalNotes.text: Lilium candidum has a long history in cultivation and European cultural imagery. Its common names include Madonna lily and Annunciation lily.

culturalNotes.title: A flower with multiple cultural meanings
culturalNotes.text: Smithsonian Libraries describes lilies as culturally complex: white forms have been associated with innocence, chastity and purity of heart, while other lily colours and contexts have carried different associations.

symbolism: purity — in particular European Christian and Victorian traditions
innocence — documented in historical flower symbolism
chastity — documented in historical religious and floral symbolism
renewal or life — in some cultural contexts, especially where the lily appears in life-cycle imagery
flowers.sundayGardenInterpretation: White Lily is a reminder that being gentle does not require being fragile. Its whiteness can be read as a quiet visual language of clarity and sincerity, while the botanical reality beneath that appearance is more varied: many different lilies can bloom white. In Sunday Garden, that becomes a small distinction worth keeping — what we see may be simple, while the life behind it can be much more complex.

distribution.nativeRange: The genus Lilium is native from temperate parts of the Northern Hemisphere to the northern Philippines, with major diversity in Eastern Asia. Exact ranges differ by species.
distribution.introducedElsewhere: Individual Lilium species and cultivars are widely cultivated outside their native ranges.
distribution.distributionNote: Because White Lily is a category rather than a species, no single native range should be assigned to the Gardener’s flower.

habitatProfile.habitat: Species of Lilium occupy varied habitats; cultivated lilies occur in gardens, borders and containers, while wild species occur in diverse temperate environments.
habitatProfile.growthEnvironment: RHS notes that cultivated lilies generally prefer moist, well-drained soil, with site preferences varying among species.

flowering.pattern: Flowering varies substantially by species and cultivar; cultivated lilies are commonly summer-flowering, while exact timing depends on the taxon and climate.
flowering.note: Do not infer the flowering season of the Gardener’s White Lily without a species or cultivar identification.

reproduction.sexual: Flowers can reproduce through pollination and seed formation; the resulting capsule contains seeds.
reproduction.vegetative: Lilies can also be propagated vegetatively, including by offsets in appropriate taxa and cultivation systems.

lifeCycle.summary: Perennial bulb → seasonal shoot and leaf growth → flowering → seed development where pollinated → dormancy/rest period → renewed growth.

ecology.pollination: Flower shape, scent and nectar-related structures vary among Lilium species and can interact with different pollinators.
ecology.role: Lilium flowers contribute nectar and pollen resources within their native ecosystems, while cultivated forms function primarily as ornamental plants.

conservation.status: No single conservation status applies to “White Lily” as a category. Conservation status must be assessed species by species.
conservation.note: Kew lists Lilium candidum as an accepted species and provides species-level distribution and conservation information; this cannot be generalized to all white-flowered lilies.

phases.name: Phase 01
phases.description: The plant persists underground as a bulb through an annual cycle of growth.

phases.name: Phase 02
phases.description: A leafy stem emerges from the bulb and develops its characteristic foliage.

phases.name: Phase 03
phases.description: Flowers form toward the end of the stem, with shape, fragrance, number and flowering season varying among species and cultivars.

phases.name: Phase 04
phases.description: After flowering, fertilised flowers can develop capsules and seeds while the plant replenishes its underground reserves for the next growth cycle.

flowers.taxonomicNote: Pink & White Lily is a descriptive colour/pattern category, not a single species. The genus Lilium contains many species and cultivars with white flowers, pink flushing, spots, stripes, or combinations of colours.

morphology.roots: Roots develop from the bulb and stem base; some lilies also produce roots along the lower stem.
morphology.stem: Erect, leafy stems arise from the bulb.
morphology.leaves: Leaves may be arranged alternately, spirally, or in whorls depending on species.
morphology.flower: Flowers can be trumpet-, bowl-, funnel-, or Turk’s-cap-shaped; colours include white, pink and many combinations.

interestingFacts.title: The colour combination is real
interestingFacts.text: RHS documents Lilium regale with white trumpet flowers flushed with pink and Lilium Muscadet with white flowers carrying a pink flush and dark pink speckles.

interestingFacts.title: It is not one species
interestingFacts.text: The label Pink & White Lily can describe multiple Lilium species and cultivated selections.

interestingFacts.title: Lily flowers are highly diverse
interestingFacts.text: RHS describes trumpet, bowl, funnel-shaped and Turk’s-cap flowers across the genus, with colours ranging from white and pastels to bold bicolours.

culturalNotes.title: A category rather than a historical name
culturalNotes.text: Pink & White Lily is treated here as a visual category. Cultural associations should therefore be attached to documented species, traditions, artworks or flower-language sources rather than presented as a universal meaning.

symbolism: beauty and affection in selected flower-language traditions
purity or innocence in traditions associated with white lilies
personal meaning defined by the Gardener
flowers.sundayGardenInterpretation: Pink and white can coexist without one needing to erase the other. For Sunday Garden, the flower becomes a quiet reminder that tenderness and clarity can share the same petals, while the meaning ultimately belongs to the person who chose it.

distribution.nativeRange: The genus Lilium is native across parts of the Northern Hemisphere, including Europe, Asia and North America; the exact range depends on species.
distribution.introducedElsewhere: Many lilies are cultivated well outside their native ranges.
distribution.distributionNote: Because Pink & White Lily is a category, distribution is described at genus level rather than assigned to a single species.

habitatProfile.habitat: Species of Lilium occupy varied habitats, from woodland and mountain settings to open grassland and garden environments.
habitatProfile.growthEnvironment: Cultivated lilies generally prefer suitable drainage and light conditions appropriate to the species or cultivar.

flowering.flowerPosition: Flowers are borne toward the upper portions of erect leafy stems.
flowering.flowerSize: Varies widely by species and cultivar.
flowering.colour: White flowers may be flushed, spotted or otherwise marked with pink; RHS documents multiple examples.

reproduction.flowers: Flowers contain stamens and carpels characteristic of Lilium.
reproduction.seeds: Seeds are produced within the capsules.
reproduction.note: Cultivated lilies can also be propagated vegetatively, including by offsets in suitable types.

lifeCycle.persistence: Most garden lilies are bulbous perennials with seasonal growth and dormancy.
lifeCycle.seasonalityNote: Flowering time varies by species, group, cultivar and climate.

ecology.role: Flowering bulbous plants that interact with their surrounding habitat through flowers, foliage, roots and underground storage organs.
ecology.caution: No single pollinator or ecological role is assigned to the entire genus because species differ.

conservation.note: No single conservation status is assigned because Pink & White Lily is not one taxon. Conservation needs should be evaluated at species or cultivar level where relevant.

phases.name: Phase 01
phases.description: The bulb stores resources during dormant periods.

phases.name: Phase 02
phases.description: New stems and leaves emerge from the bulb during the active growing season.

phases.name: Phase 03
phases.description: Flowers develop at the top of the leafy stem, with form and colour varying by species or cultivar.

phases.name: Phase 04
phases.description: After flowering, the plant replenishes the bulb before foliage dies back in many deciduous lilies.
